cards.title: Polylogarithmic treewidth with forbidden induced minors
cards.formal: For every integer t≥2, does there exist an integer c_t≥1 such that every n-vertex graph G with n≥2, no clique of size t and neither Kt,t nor Wt as an induced minor satisfies tw(G)≤c_t(log₂ n)^(c_t)?
cards.why: Would yield a substantially stronger structural bound for graphs excluding two induced-minor patterns and large cliques. Polylogarithmic treewidth supports quasipolynomial algorithms for many problems whose dependence on treewidth is exponential, making the quantitative improvement algorithmically significant.
cards.status_note: Original question and the unambiguous March 2026 formulation checked, with searches through 11 September 2026. The subpolynomial and coarse-decomposition results do not resolve the stated polylogarithmic treewidth target. Preprint theorem statements were matched to the model; proofs were not independently verified.

sentences: Treewidth measures the largest bag needed to organize a graph in a tree decomposition.
The question concerns graphs with no large clique and with neither a fixed complete bipartite graph nor a fixed wall as an induced minor.
It asks whether their treewidth is bounded by a fixed power of the logarithm of their number of vertices.
A March 2026 preprint proves a subpolynomial bound but still states the polylogarithmic target as a conjecture.
The stronger bound would improve the structural and algorithmic understanding of these induced-minor-free graph classes.

cards.definitions: All graphs are finite, undirected and simple. Write n=|V(G)| and take logarithms in base two. An induced subgraph G[S] retains precisely all edges of G whose endpoints are in S. Kt is the complete graph on t vertices; Kt,t is the complete bipartite graph with two independent sets of t vertices and every edge between the sets. A tree decomposition consists of a finite tree T and bags Bx⊆V(G), one per node x of T, such that every vertex occurs in a bag, both endpoints of every edge occur together in some bag, and the bags containing any fixed vertex form a connected subtree of T. Its width is maxx |Bx|−1. Treewidth tw(G) is the minimum width of such a decomposition. For a concrete wall convention, construct Wt from vertices (i,j), 0≤i≤t and 0≤j≤2t+1: include all horizontal edges (i,j)(i,j+1), and vertical edges (i,j)(i+1,j) exactly when i+j is even, then repeatedly delete vertices of degree at most one until none remain. This is a fixed elementary hexagonal-wall family. Standard wall-size conventions differ by a fixed reindexing; since the source statement quantifies over every fixed t and allows its constants to depend arbitrarily on t, this indexing does not change the family-level claim. An induced minor is obtained by deleting vertices and contracting edges, with loops discarded and parallel edges merged, but without arbitrary edge deletions. Equivalently, its vertices can be represented by pairwise disjoint nonempty connected branch sets in G, with an edge between two branch sets exactly when their corresponding vertices are adjacent in the induced minor. The clique exclusion is an ordinary clique/induced-subgraph condition; the exclusions of Kt,t and Wt are induced-minor conditions. There is no bound on maximum degree. The constant c_t and the exponent c_t may depend on t, but not on n or G. Allowing separate constants for the multiplier and exponent is equivalent by increasing c_t, since log₂ n≥1. The statement is structural existence of tree decompositions and requests no algorithm for finding them. Restricting to t,n≥2 removes only trivial small or undefined-log cases.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed bound for every t with constants depending only on t, or refute it by finding one fixed t for which, for every integer c≥1, there is an admitted graph G with tw(G)>c(log₂ |V(G)|)^c. A subpolynomial upper bound or a bound on independence number inside bags does not establish the requested polylogarithmic bound on bag size.

context_blocks.title: Treewidth measures the size of the pieces
context_blocks.text: A tree decomposition organizes overlapping vertex sets along a tree. Vertices may appear in several bags, but their occurrences must remain connected. A path has treewidth one, whereas a complete graph on n vertices has treewidth n−1. Small bags allow many graph problems to be processed through their interactions along the decomposition.

context_blocks.title: Which large structures are excluded
context_blocks.text: The question removes large cliques and two specific induced-minor patterns: a complete bipartite graph and a hexagonal wall. Induced minors permit edge contractions but preserve the presence of edges between surviving branch sets. This makes their exclusion different from forbidding an ordinary graph minor, where arbitrary edges may also be deleted.

context_blocks.title: A polylogarithmic target
context_blocks.text: For each fixed t, the requested bound is a constant times a fixed power of log n. The power can grow with t. The statement does not ask for a constant treewidth bound and does not impose the maximum-degree restriction of the separate logarithmic-degree question.

context_blocks.title: Subpolynomial progress leaves a gap
context_blocks.text: The March 2026 version of Chudnovsky and coauthors’ preprint states tw(G)≤2^(a_t(log₂ n)^(1−ε_t)) for constants a_t and ε_t>0 under these same exclusions. It states the polylogarithmic bound separately as Conjecture 1.1. The reported upper bound is subpolynomial in n, but does not establish that conjecture.

context_blocks.title: Other bag measures have different meanings
context_blocks.text: The May 2026 coarse-decomposition preprint bounds how many vertices in a bag can be far apart in the original graph. A bag can contain many nearby vertices while that number remains small. Such bounds are not bounds on the number of vertices in the bag, which is what treewidth counts.

cards.title: Logarithmic treewidth for t-clean graphs of logarithmic degree
cards.formal: For every integer t≥2, does there exist an integer c_t≥1 such that every t-clean graph G on n≥2 vertices with maximum degree Δ(G)≤log₂ n satisfies tw(G)≤c_t log₂ n?
cards.why: Would turn a logarithmic maximum-degree bound into logarithmic decomposition width within a substantial induced-subgraph class. That quantitative threshold can support polynomial-time algorithms for problems with single-exponential dependence on treewidth, where a higher polylogarithmic width generally gives a weaker runtime guarantee.
cards.status_note: Full original question and corrected 2024 partial result checked. Subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026 located no resolution of the exact logarithmic bound under all the source’s hypotheses. Related stronger or differently measured decomposition claims were not substituted for it. Proofs were not independently audited.

progress.text: Chudnovsky poses the exact c(t) log n bound for t-clean graphs of maximum degree at most log n.

The corrected Bonnet–Hodor–Korhonen–Masařík preprint gives a polylogarithmic bound through polynomial dependence on maximum degree, with the necessary weak-sparsity hypothesis. It identifies the logarithmic bound as still beyond its result.

sentences: The question concerns t-clean graphs, which exclude four specified kinds of induced subgraphs including subdivided walls and their line graphs.
It additionally assumes that every vertex has degree at most the logarithm of the graph’s number of vertices.
The requested conclusion is treewidth at most a t-dependent constant times that same logarithm.
The corrected 2024 partial result yields a polylogarithmic bound, which can have a larger exponent.
A logarithmic bound would improve both the decomposition structure and the algorithmic consequences for these graphs.

cards.definitions: All graphs are finite, undirected and simple. Write n=|V(G)| and take logarithms in base two. An induced subgraph G[S] retains precisely all edges of G whose endpoints are in S. Kt is the complete graph on t vertices; Kt,t is the complete bipartite graph with two independent sets of t vertices and every edge between the sets. A tree decomposition consists of a finite tree T and bags Bx⊆V(G), one per node x of T, such that every vertex occurs in a bag, both endpoints of every edge occur together in some bag, and the bags containing any fixed vertex form a connected subtree of T. Its width is maxx |Bx|−1. Treewidth tw(G) is the minimum width of such a decomposition. For a concrete wall convention, construct Wt from vertices (i,j), 0≤i≤t and 0≤j≤2t+1: include all horizontal edges (i,j)(i,j+1), and vertical edges (i,j)(i+1,j) exactly when i+j is even, then repeatedly delete vertices of degree at most one until none remain. This is a fixed elementary hexagonal-wall family. Standard wall-size conventions differ by a fixed reindexing; since the source statement quantifies over every fixed t and allows its constants to depend arbitrarily on t, this indexing does not change the family-level claim. A subdivision of a graph replaces each edge by a path of at least one edge, with all new internal vertices distinct; the original graph is allowed. The line graph L(H) has one vertex for each edge of H, with two vertices adjacent exactly when the corresponding edges share an endpoint. A graph is t-clean if none of its induced subgraphs is isomorphic to Kt, Kt,t, any subdivision H of Wt, or the line graph L(H) of any such subdivision. All four exclusions are induced-subgraph exclusions, with every subdivision quantified over. Maximum degree Δ(G) is the largest number of neighbors of a vertex of G. The same constant c_t must work for all admitted graphs and sizes; it may depend on t only. Logarithms use base two, and the claim is unaffected by standard logarithm/wall conventions after changing the t-dependent constants and reindexing the fixed obstructions. No vertex partition or algorithmic output is requested.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed logarithmic treewidth bound for every fixed t, or refute it by finding a fixed t for which tw(G)/log₂ |V(G)| is unbounded among t-clean graphs satisfying Δ(G)≤log₂ |V(G)|. A bound by (log n)^a with a>1 does not meet the target. A counterexample must retain all four induced-subgraph exclusions and the maximum-degree promise.

context_blocks.title: Low degree alone is insufficient
context_blocks.text: Degree is local: it counts neighbors of a single vertex. Treewidth measures how large the pieces must be in a global decomposition. An r-by-r square grid has maximum degree at most four but treewidth r, so bounded degree alone does not force logarithmic treewidth in the number r² of vertices.

context_blocks.title: What t-clean rules out
context_blocks.text: The four forbidden patterns cover complete graphs, complete bipartite graphs, subdivided walls and the line graphs of subdivided walls. The exclusions are induced: all edges among the selected vertices matter. The maximum-degree promise is an additional condition on the whole graph.

context_blocks.title: A linear dependence on log n
context_blocks.text: The constant multiplier can depend arbitrarily on the fixed forbidden-pattern size t. The dependence on n must be at most c_t log n. This is stronger than a polylogarithmic estimate with an unspecified exponent, even though both grow slowly.

context_blocks.title: The corrected 2024 partial result
context_blocks.text: Bonnet, Hodor, Korhonen and Masařík prove a polynomial bound in maximum degree for graphs excluding a fixed biclique as a subgraph and a fixed planar graph as an induced minor. Their discussion relates this to Chudnovsky’s t-clean formulation and obtains a polylogarithmic bound when degree is O(log n). It explicitly leaves the logarithmic bound beyond that result.

context_blocks.title: Why the revision matters
context_blocks.text: The 2024 paper records that its first version omitted the biclique hypothesis because of a flawed intermediate lemma. The corrected theorem retains that hypothesis. The present card uses the corrected statement and the source’s original four exclusions.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
